Maximum Energy of Integral Circulant Graphs with Same-Parity Exponents

Jianwei Jiang ††thanks: Email: jianweijiangwf@sina.com Affiliation: School of Mathematics and Statistics, Weifang University,    Chunhua Yang ††thanks: Corresponding author. Email: chunhuayangwf@sina.com Affiliation: Weifang, Shandong, China
Abstract

The energy of a finite graph is the sum of the absolute values of the eigenvalues of its adjacency matrix. Let n=pa​qbn=p^{a}q^{b}, where p,q≥5p,q\geq 5 are distinct primes and a,b≥1a,b\geq 1 have the same parity. Among all nonempty sets 𝒟\mathcal{D} of proper divisors of nn, the energy of the corresponding integral circulant graph is maximised by exactly two divisor sets: the divisors pi​qjp^{i}q^{j} with i+ji+j odd, and the divisors with i+ji+j even after removing pa​qbp^{a}q^{b}. The maximum energy is

ℰmax​(n)=12​[n+da​(p)​db​(q)−2​ga​(p)​gb​(q)],\mathcal{E}_{\max}(n)=\frac{1}{2}\left[n+d_{a}(p)d_{b}(q)-2g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q)\right],

where

dk​(x)=(2​k+1)​xk+4​∑j=0k−1(−1)k−j​(j+1)​xj,gk​(x)=xk​(x−1)+2​(−1)kx+1.d_{k}(x)=(2k+1)x^{k}+4\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^{k-j}(j+1)x^{j},\qquad g_{k}(x)=\frac{x^{k}(x-1)+2(-1)^{k}}{x+1}.

For the proof, weighted prime-power Ramanujan transforms yield an exact tensor-product representation of the graph energy, reducing the extremal problem to a weighted cut separating two prescribed vertices. After a sign conjugation, the relevant transforms decompose into embedded path blocks; the nontrivial blocks correspond to a weighted path together with 33-chords of weight −1-1. We prove a sharp lower bound for cuts separating the two prescribed vertices in Kronecker products of these path blocks. For products of two such nontrivial blocks, equality holds only for cuts that isolate one of the two prescribed vertices. Combined with the energy-to-cut correspondence, these equality cases yield exactly the two maximising divisor sets.

Keywords. Graph energy; integral circulant graph; Ramanujan sum; Kronecker product; weighted cut.

2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. 05C50; 11A25; 15A18.

1 Introduction

Let GG be a finite graph with adjacency eigenvalues λ1,…,λn\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{n}. Its energy is ℰ⁡(G)=∑j=1n|λj|\mathcal{E}(G)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}|\lambda_{j}|; see Li, Shi and Gutman [5]. For an integer n>1n>1 and a nonempty set 𝒟\mathcal{D} of proper divisors of nn, let ICGn⁡(𝒟)\operatorname{ICG}_{n}(\mathcal{D}) be the graph on ℤ/n​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} in which distinct vertices u,vu,v are adjacent exactly when gcd⁡(u−v,n)∈𝒟\gcd(u-v,n)\in\mathcal{D}. By So [8], these are precisely the integral circulant graphs with at least one edge.

The extremal-energy problem for integral circulant graphs is best understood in the prime-power setting. Sander and Sander obtained an explicit formula for the energy and later gave a complete description of the maximum energy together with all divisor sets attaining it [6, 7]. For orders involving more than one prime factor, the picture is less complete: Le and Sander [4] used multiplicative divisor sets to obtain bounds on the minimum and maximum energies. Earlier work of Ilić and Bašić [2] provided explicit formulas for the energy of several families of integral circulant graphs and also addressed the corresponding minimum-energy problem.

In our earlier work [3], we determined the maximum energy of integral circulant graphs of order n=p2​r​q2​s+1n=p^{2r}q^{2s+1}, where p,qp,q are distinct odd primes, q≥5q\geq 5, r≥1r\geq 1, and s≥0s\geq 0, and proved that the even checkerboard divisor set is the unique maximiser. In the notation of Section 2, with a=2​ra=2r and b=2​s+1b=2s+1, the proof is based on

2​ℰ​(ICGn⁡(𝒟))=‖n​et+K​y‖1≤n+‖K​y‖1≤n+da​(p)​db​(q),2\mathcal{E}(\operatorname{ICG}_{n}(\mathcal{D}))=\|ne_{t}+Ky\|_{1}\leq n+\|Ky\|_{1}\leq n+d_{a}(p)d_{b}(q),

where dk​(x)d_{k}(x) is defined below. For opposite-parity exponents, both inequalities can hold with equality. When aa and bb have the same parity, equality in the second inequality is still attained by the corresponding checkerboard vector, but for this vector (K​y)t<0(Ky)_{t}<0. Since n​etne_{t} is positive only at tt, cancellation occurs in the last coordinate and the first inequality is strict. Accordingly, in this paper we directly maximise 12​‖n​et+K​y‖1\frac{1}{2}\|ne_{t}+Ky\|_{1}.

For k≥1k\geq 1 and x>1x>1, put

dk​(x)=(2​k+1)​xk+4​∑j=0k−1(−1)k−j​(j+1)​xj,gk​(x)=xk​(x−1)+2​(−1)kx+1.d_{k}(x)=(2k+1)x^{k}+4\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^{k-j}(j+1)x^{j},\qquad g_{k}(x)=\frac{x^{k}(x-1)+2(-1)^{k}}{x+1}.

The function gkg_{k} is also a polynomial: gk​(x)=xk+2​∑j=0k−1(−1)k−j​xjg_{k}(x)=x^{k}+2\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(-1)^{k-j}x^{j}. The quantities dk​(x)d_{k}(x) and gk​(x)g_{k}(x) are, respectively, the trace and the last diagonal entry of the diagonal weight matrix used in [3, Section 3.1].

Theorem A.

Let p,q≥5p,q\geq 5 be distinct primes, and let a,b≥1a,b\geq 1 be integers with a+ba+b even. Put n=pa​qbn=p^{a}q^{b}. Among all nonempty sets 𝒟\mathcal{D} of proper divisors of nn, the maximum energy of ICGn⁡(𝒟)\operatorname{ICG}_{n}(\mathcal{D}) is

ℰmax​(n)=12​[n+da​(p)​db​(q)−2​ga​(p)​gb​(q)].\mathcal{E}_{\max}(n)=\frac{1}{2}\left[n+d_{a}(p)d_{b}(q)-2g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q)\right]. (1.1)

Exactly two divisor sets attain this value:

𝒟odd\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{odd}} ={piqj:0≤i≤a, 0≤j≤b,i+j odd},\displaystyle=\{p^{i}q^{j}:0\leq i\leq a,\ 0\leq j\leq b,\ i+j\text{ odd}\}, (1.2)
𝒟even−\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{even}}^{-} ={piqj:0≤i≤a, 0≤j≤b,i+j even}∖{paqb}.\displaystyle=\{p^{i}q^{j}:0\leq i\leq a,\ 0\leq j\leq b,\ i+j\text{ even}\}\setminus\{p^{a}q^{b}\}.

The two sets in (1.2) partition the proper divisors of nn, so the corresponding graphs are complementary. Together with [3], Theorem A determines the maximum energy and all maximising divisor sets for every order pa​qbp^{a}q^{b}, where p,q≥5p,q\geq 5 are distinct primes and a,b≥1a,b\geq 1.

To analyse the cancellation retained in the exact objective, we depart from the semidefinite argument of [3] while retaining its weighted Ramanujan transform framework. After a sign conjugation, we convert the problem into a weighted cut problem in which two prescribed vertices lie on opposite sides of the cut. The sign-conjugated prime-power transforms are decomposed into embedded path blocks, together with an additional last-coordinate term in the even-exponent case. Each nontrivial block is supported on a weighted path with 33-chords of weight −1-1. The contribution of each negative 33-chord is transferred to the three edges of its associated path, leaving nonnegative correction terms and reducing the cut estimate to a residual weighted product graph. We then establish a sharp lower bound and characterise its equality cases for Kronecker products of two such blocks (Theorem 4.8). These blockwise estimates are lifted to the full transforms; in the even-exponent case, the strict contribution of the outermost nontrivial block controls the additional mixed terms. Combined with the energy-to-cut correspondence, this yields both the maximum in (1.1) and the two maximising divisor sets in (1.2).

2 From graph energy to a cut sum

2.1 The transforms and the divisor coordinates

For k≥1k\geq 1 and a prime pp, as in [3, Eq. (2.2)], define the weighted prime-power Ramanujan transform Tk​(p)T_{k}(p) by

(Tk​(p))u​i=φ⁡(pk−u)​cpk−i​(pu)(0≤u,i≤k),(T_{k}(p))_{ui}=\varphi(p^{k-u})c_{p^{k-i}}(p^{u})\qquad(0\leq u,i\leq k),

where φ\varphi is Euler’s totient function and chc_{h} is the Ramanujan sum. By the standard prime-power formula for Ramanujan sums [1, Section 8.3], the entries of Tk​(p)T_{k}(p) admit the following explicit polynomial expressions. We use the same formulas to define Tk​(x)T_{k}(x) for every real parameter x>1x>1; see [3, Proposition 2.1]:

(Tk​(x))i​j={0,i,j<k,i+j≤k−2,−xk−1​(x−1),i,j<k,i+j=k−1,x2​k−i−j−2​(x−1)2,i,j<k,i+j≥k,(T_{k}(x))_{ij}=\begin{cases}0,&i,j<k,\ i+j\leq k-2,\\ -x^{k-1}(x-1),&i,j<k,\ i+j=k-1,\\ x^{2k-i-j-2}(x-1)^{2},&i,j<k,\ i+j\geq k,\end{cases} (2.1)

with boundary entries

(Tk​(x))i​k=(Tk​(x))k​i=xk−i−1​(x−1)(i<k),(Tk​(x))k​k=1.(T_{k}(x))_{ik}=(T_{k}(x))_{ki}=x^{k-i-1}(x-1)\quad(i<k),\qquad(T_{k}(x))_{kk}=1. (2.2)

In particular, Tk​(x)T_{k}(x) is symmetric and

Tk​(x)​𝟏=xk​ek.T_{k}(x)\mathbf{1}=x^{k}e_{k}. (2.3)

Here and below, eke_{k} is the last standard basis vector and 𝟏\mathbf{1} is an all-one vector of the required size.

Let sk=(1,−1,…,(−1)k)𝖳s_{k}=(1,-1,\ldots,(-1)^{k})^{\mathsf{T}} and Sk=diag⁡(sk)S_{k}=\operatorname{diag}(s_{k}). We also use the diagonal matrix Δk​(x)\Delta_{k}(x) introduced in [3, Section 3.1]. The following properties of Δk​(x)\Delta_{k}(x) will be used below; see [3, Lemma 3.1 and equations (3.4), (3.6)–(3.7)]:

Tk​(x)​sk=(−1)k​Δk​(x)​sk,tr⁡Δk​(x)=dk​(x),(Δk​(x))k​k=gk​(x).T_{k}(x)s_{k}=(-1)^{k}\Delta_{k}(x)s_{k},\qquad\operatorname{tr}\Delta_{k}(x)=d_{k}(x),\qquad(\Delta_{k}(x))_{kk}=g_{k}(x). (2.4)

For x≥5x\geq 5, Δk​(x)\Delta_{k}(x) is a positive diagonal matrix; see [3, Section 3.1].

Fix distinct primes p,q≥5p,q\geq 5 and positive integers a,ba,b, and set

n=pa​qb,ℐ={0,…,a}×{0,…,b},t=(a,b),N=(a+1)​(b+1).n=p^{a}q^{b},\qquad\mathcal{I}=\{0,\ldots,a\}\times\{0,\ldots,b\},\qquad t=(a,b),\qquad N=(a+1)(b+1).

Vectors indexed by ℐ\mathcal{I} are ordered by ι⁡(i,j)=i+(a+1)​j\iota(i,j)=i+(a+1)j, so the first coordinate varies fastest. A divisor set is encoded by a binary matrix X=(xi​j)X=(x_{ij}), where xi​j=1x_{ij}=1 precisely when pi​qj∈𝒟p^{i}q^{j}\in\mathcal{D}. Write x=vec⁡(X)x=\operatorname{vec}(X) in this order and put

y=2​x−𝟏,x=12​(𝟏+y).y=2x-\mathbf{1},\qquad x=\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{1}+y). (2.5)

The proper-divisor condition is xt=0x_{t}=0, or equivalently yt=−1y_{t}=-1. We allow the empty divisor set in intermediate upper bounds; the corresponding graph has energy zero.

Define

K=Tb(q)⊗Ta(p),Δ=Δb(q)⊗Δa(p),s=sb⊗sa,S=Sb⊗Sa=diag(s),τ=da(p)db(q),γ=ga(p)gb(q).\begin{gathered}K=T_{b}(q)\otimes T_{a}(p),\qquad\Delta=\Delta_{b}(q)\otimes\Delta_{a}(p),\\ s=s_{b}\otimes s_{a},\qquad S=S_{b}\otimes S_{a}=\operatorname{diag}(s),\qquad\tau=d_{a}(p)d_{b}(q),\qquad\gamma=g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q).\end{gathered}

Thus si,j=(−1)i+js_{i,j}=(-1)^{i+j} and Δt​t=γ\Delta_{tt}=\gamma. With the above ordering, the standard vectorisation identity vec⁡(A​X​B𝖳)=(B⊗A)​vec⁡(X)\operatorname{vec}(AXB^{\mathsf{T}})=(B\otimes A)\operatorname{vec}(X) gives K​x=vec⁡(Ta​(p)​X​Tb​(q)𝖳)Kx=\operatorname{vec}\!\bigl(T_{a}(p)XT_{b}(q)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigr). Hence, by the energy formula in [3, Proposition 2.2], ℰ⁡(ICGn⁡(𝒟))=‖K​x‖1\mathcal{E}(\operatorname{ICG}_{n}(\mathcal{D}))=\|Kx\|_{1}. Also, by (2.3),

K​𝟏=(Tb​(q)​𝟏)⊗(Ta​(p)​𝟏)=qb​eb⊗pa​ea=n​et.K\mathbf{1}=(T_{b}(q)\mathbf{1})\otimes(T_{a}(p)\mathbf{1})=q^{b}e_{b}\otimes p^{a}e_{a}=ne_{t}. (2.6)

Combining (2.5) and (2.6) gives

2​ℰ​(ICGn⁡(𝒟))=‖K⁡(𝟏+y)‖1=‖n​et+K​y‖1=:F⁡(y).2\mathcal{E}(\operatorname{ICG}_{n}(\mathcal{D}))=\|K(\mathbf{1}+y)\|_{1}=\|ne_{t}+Ky\|_{1}=:F(y). (2.7)

2.2 The prescribed terminals

For k≥1k\geq 1 and x>1x>1 put

𝖡k​(x)=(−1)k​Sk​Tk​(x)​Sk.\mathsf{B}_{k}(x)=(-1)^{k}S_{k}T_{k}(x)S_{k}. (2.8)

Since Sk​𝟏=skS_{k}\mathbf{1}=s_{k}, the first identity in (2.4) gives

𝖡k​(x)​𝟏=(−1)k​Sk​Tk​(x)​sk=Sk​Δk​(x)​sk=Δk​(x)​Sk​sk=Δk​(x)​𝟏.\mathsf{B}_{k}(x)\mathbf{1}=(-1)^{k}S_{k}T_{k}(x)s_{k}=S_{k}\Delta_{k}(x)s_{k}=\Delta_{k}(x)S_{k}s_{k}=\Delta_{k}(x)\mathbf{1}. (2.9)

Here SkS_{k} and Δk​(x)\Delta_{k}(x) commute because both are diagonal, and Sk​sk=𝟏S_{k}s_{k}=\mathbf{1}. In particular, the last row sum of 𝖡k​(x)\mathsf{B}_{k}(x) is gk​(x)g_{k}(x). We now use the assumption that a+ba+b is even. Put C=S​K​SC=SKS. Then

C=𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p),C​𝟏=Δ​𝟏,∑u,v∈ℐCu​v=τ.C=\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p),\qquad C\mathbf{1}=\Delta\mathbf{1},\qquad\sum_{u,v\in\mathcal{I}}C_{uv}=\tau. (2.10)

The first equality follows from the mixed-product property and the scalar identity (α​A)⊗(β​B)=α​β​(A⊗B)(\alpha A)\otimes(\beta B)=\alpha\beta(A\otimes B), together with the definition of 𝖡k​(x)\mathsf{B}_{k}(x) and (−1)a+b=1(-1)^{a+b}=1. The second follows by right-multiplying the first by 𝟏=𝟏b+1⊗𝟏a+1\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}_{b+1}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{a+1}, using the mixed-product property and (2.9). Left-multiplying the second by 𝟏𝖳\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf{T}}, and using that Δ\Delta is diagonal together with tr⁡(A⊗B)=tr⁡(A)​tr⁡(B)\operatorname{tr}(A\otimes B)=\operatorname{tr}(A)\operatorname{tr}(B), gives the third. Since t=(a,b)t=(a,b) is the last index in the above ordering, taking the tt-th coordinate of C​𝟏=Δ​𝟏C\mathbf{1}=\Delta\mathbf{1} gives ∑v∈ℐCt​v=Δt​t=γ\sum_{v\in\mathcal{I}}C_{tv}=\Delta_{tt}=\gamma. Thus the last row sum of CC is γ\gamma. Since CC is symmetric, its last column sum is also γ\gamma.

Regard Cu​vC_{uv} as the weight of an edge from row vertex uu to column vertex vv. Row and column vertices are separate copies of ℐ\mathcal{I}; even Ct​tC_{tt} joins two different vertices. For sign vectors ζ,ξ∈{±1}N\zeta,\xi\in\{\pm 1\}^{N}, define

cutC(ζ,ξ)=∑u,v∈ℐCu​v𝟏{ζu≠ξv}.\operatorname{cut}_{C}(\zeta,\xi)=\sum_{u,v\in\mathcal{I}}C_{uv}\mathbf{1}_{\{\zeta_{u}\neq\xi_{v}\}}. (2.11)

Some weights may be negative. The quantity in (2.11) is the sum of the weights crossing the sign partition. We consider cuts satisfying

ζt=1,ξt=−1.\zeta_{t}=1,\qquad\xi_{t}=-1. (2.12)

The two vertices indexed by tt are called the terminals. The terminal cuts are the cuts that isolate one of them:

(ζ,ξ)=(−𝟏+2​et,−𝟏)or(ζ,ξ)=(𝟏,𝟏−2​et).(\zeta,\xi)=(-\mathbf{1}+2e_{t},-\mathbf{1})\quad\text{or}\quad(\zeta,\xi)=(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1}-2e_{t}). (2.13)

Since the entries in the last row and last column of CC each sum to γ\gamma, both terminal cuts have weight γ\gamma.

For a fixed y∈{±1}Ny\in\{\pm 1\}^{N} with yt=−1y_{t}=-1, put ξ=S​y\xi=Sy. Then

and the only maximising vectors are −s-s and s−2​ets-2e_{t}.

By Lemma 2.1, it remains to prove that every cut of CC satisfying (2.12) has weight at least γ\gamma, with equality only for the two terminal cuts in (2.13). Since (2.10) gives C=𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)C=\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p), we first decompose the factors 𝖡k​(x)\mathsf{B}_{k}(x). The resulting nontrivial matrices will be represented by weighted paths in Section 4, where the required cut bounds for their Kronecker products are established.

3 Decomposing a transform into path matrices

For a (j+1)×(j+1)(j+1)\times(j+1) matrix AA and k≥jk\geq j, let 𝒥k,j​(A)\mathcal{J}_{k,j}(A) be the (k+1)×(k+1)(k+1)\times(k+1) matrix with AA in its lower-right block on coordinates k−j,…,kk-j,\ldots,k and zero elsewhere. In particular, the last row and last column of AA are embedded in the last row and last column of the larger matrix. Put 𝖤k=ek​ek𝖳\mathsf{E}_{k}=e_{k}e_{k}^{\mathsf{T}} and define

(𝖯k)i​j=𝟏{i+j=k−1 or i+j=k}(0≤i,j≤k),𝖯0=[1].(\mathsf{P}_{k})_{ij}=\mathbf{1}_{\{i+j=k-1\text{ or }i+j=k\}}\quad(0\leq i,j\leq k),\qquad\mathsf{P}_{0}=[1]. (3.1)

For j≥1j\geq 1 and a real number cc, set

𝖧j​(c)=c​𝖯j−𝒥j,j−1​(𝖯j−1).\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)=c\mathsf{P}_{j}-\mathcal{J}_{j,j-1}(\mathsf{P}_{j-1}). (3.2)

For a square matrix AA with a designated last coordinate, write h⁡(A)h(A) for its last row sum. The definitions give

h⁡(𝖯j)=1,h⁡(𝖧j​(c))=c−1,h⁡(𝖤k)=1.h(\mathsf{P}_{j})=1,\qquad h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c))=c-1,\qquad h(\mathsf{E}_{k})=1. (3.3)

The same sums hold for the last columns, because these matrices are symmetric.

Lemma 3.1.

Set 𝖡0​(x)=[1]\mathsf{B}_{0}(x)=[1]. For k≥1k\geq 1 and x>1x>1,

𝖡k​(x)=xk−1​(x−1)​𝖯k−𝒥k,k−1​(𝖡k−1​(x)).\mathsf{B}_{k}(x)=x^{k-1}(x-1)\mathsf{P}_{k}-\mathcal{J}_{k,k-1}(\mathsf{B}_{k-1}(x)). (3.4)

On the last row or column, let the other index satisfy 1≤i≤k−11\leq i\leq k-1. By (2.8) and (2.2), at position (k,i)(k,i), (𝖡k)k,i=(−1)i​xk−i−1​(x−1)(\mathsf{B}_{k})_{k,i}=(-1)^{i}x^{k-i-1}(x-1). Now let k≥2k\geq 2. Substitute (3.4) for 𝖡k−1\mathsf{B}_{k-1}. The first two terms combine as

We suppress ζ,ξ\zeta,\xi when the cut is fixed. The expression is linear in each matrix argument.

4 Cut bounds for products of path matrices

4.1 Short edges and 3-chords

Path representation.

We represent 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} by the path

0−1−⋯−(2​j+1).0-1-\cdots-(2j+1).

Indeed, as ℓ\ell ranges from 00 to jj, place column ℓ\ell at position 2​ℓ+12\ell+1; as ii ranges from 00 to jj, place row ii at position 2​(j−i)2(j-i). Together these positions are exactly 0,1,…,2​j+10,1,\ldots,2j+1. By (3.1), for each ii, row ii is adjacent precisely to columns j−i−1j-i-1 and j−ij-i, whenever these indices lie in range. Since column ℓ\ell is placed at position 2​ℓ+12\ell+1, the corresponding column vertices are located at 2​(j−i)−12(j-i)-1 and 2​(j−i)+12(j-i)+1. Since row ii is placed at position 2​(j−i)2(j-i), these are precisely the two neighbouring positions of the row vertex on the path, with the out-of-range case omitted at the endpoints. As ii and ℓ\ell range over 0,…,j0,\ldots,j, respectively, these row and column vertices, together with the adjacencies above, give exactly this path. We call the edges of this path the short edges. The endpoints 00 and 2​j+12j+1 correspond to row jj and column jj, respectively, and hence are exactly the two terminals.

Lemma 4.1.

For j≥1j\geq 1 and real cc, the edges of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) in the above path representation are

endpointsrangeweight(2​u,2​u+1)u=0,jc(2​u,2​u+1)1≤u≤j−1c−1(2​u+1,2​u+2)0≤u≤j−1c(2​u,2​u+3)0≤u≤j−1−1.\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\text{endpoints}&\text{range}&\text{weight}\\ \hline\cr(2u,2u+1)&u=0,j&c\\ (2u,2u+1)&1\leq u\leq j-1&c-1\\ (2u+1,2u+2)&0\leq u\leq j-1&c\\ (2u,2u+3)&0\leq u\leq j-1&-1.\end{array} (4.1)

Thus, in the above path representation, 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) has the same short-edge positions as 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j}, with weight cc or c−1c-1 assigned to each such position. Those of weight cc are called S-edges, while those of weight c−1c-1 are called I-edges; when j=1j=1, there are no I-edges. Accordingly, we also call a short edge of 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} type SS or type II according as the corresponding short-edge position in 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) has weight cc or c−1c-1, respectively. In addition, 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) has the 33-chords (2​u,2​u+3)(2u,2u+3), 0≤u≤j−10\leq u\leq j-1, each of weight −1-1. Moreover, every SS-edge lies in exactly one path associated with a 33-chord, whereas every II-edge lies in exactly two such paths.

Proof.

By (3.2), 𝖧j​(c)=c​𝖯j−𝒥j,j−1​(𝖯j−1)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)=c\mathsf{P}_{j}-\mathcal{J}_{j,j-1}(\mathsf{P}_{j-1}). By (3.1),

(𝖯j)i​ℓ=1⟺i+ℓ=j−1ori+ℓ=j.(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{i\ell}=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad i+\ell=j-1\ \text{or}\ i+\ell=j. (4.2)

For the embedded term, its zeroth row and zeroth column are zero, while for 1≤i,ℓ≤j1\leq i,\ell\leq j, (𝒥j,j−1​(𝖯j−1))i​ℓ=(𝖯j−1)i−1,ℓ−1\bigl(\mathcal{J}_{j,j-1}(\mathsf{P}_{j-1})\bigr)_{i\ell}=(\mathsf{P}_{j-1})_{i-1,\ell-1}. For 1≤i,ℓ≤j1\leq i,\ell\leq j, this entry equals 11 if and only if (i−1)+(ℓ−1)=j−2(i-1)+(\ell-1)=j-2 or (i−1)+(ℓ−1)=j−1(i-1)+(\ell-1)=j-1, which is equivalent to

i+ℓ=jori+ℓ=j+1.i+\ell=j\quad\text{or}\quad i+\ell=j+1. (4.3)

We now compare (4.2) and (4.3).

If i+ℓ=j−1i+\ell=j-1, only c​𝖯jc\mathsf{P}_{j} contributes. With u=ℓu=\ell, the corresponding row and column vertices lie at 2​(j−i)=2​u+22(j-i)=2u+2 and 2​ℓ+1=2​u+12\ell+1=2u+1, respectively. Thus these are the short edges (2​u+1,2​u+2)(2u+1,2u+2), 0≤u≤j−10\leq u\leq j-1, each of weight cc.

If i+ℓ=ji+\ell=j, the corresponding short edge is (2​u,2​u+1)(2u,2u+1) with u=ℓu=\ell. For 1≤u≤j−11\leq u\leq j-1, both c​𝖯jc\mathsf{P}_{j} and the embedded term contribute, so the weight is c−1c-1. For u=0u=0 or u=ju=j, one of i,ℓi,\ell is zero, so the position lies outside the embedded block and the weight remains cc.

Finally, if i+ℓ=j+1i+\ell=j+1, then (𝖯j)i​ℓ=0(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{i\ell}=0, whereas the embedded term equals 11. With u=ℓ−1u=\ell-1, the corresponding vertices lie at 2​(j−i)=2​u2(j-i)=2u and 2​ℓ+1=2​u+32\ell+1=2u+3. Hence these positions give the 33-chords (2​u,2​u+3)(2u,2u+3), 0≤u≤j−10\leq u\leq j-1, each of weight −1-1. This proves (4.1).

It remains to count the paths containing each short edge. Two consecutive 33-chords (2​u,2​u+3)(2u,2u+3) and (2​u+2,2​u+5)(2u+2,2u+5) have the respective paths 2​u−(2​u+1)−(2​u+2)−(2​u+3)2u-(2u+1)-(2u+2)-(2u+3) and (2​u+2)−(2​u+3)−(2​u+4)−(2​u+5)(2u+2)-(2u+3)-(2u+4)-(2u+5), which share the short edge (2​u+2,2​u+3)(2u+2,2u+3). Hence every internal edge (2​v,2​v+1)(2v,2v+1), 1≤v≤j−11\leq v\leq j-1, namely every type I edge, lies in exactly two consecutive paths of this form. The remaining short edges are precisely the type S edges, and each lies in exactly one such path. This proves the final assertion. ∎

Chord replacement.

Let χe\chi_{e} be 11 when the endpoints of an edge ee have different signs and 00 otherwise. For a path with edges e1,e2,e3e_{1},e_{2},e_{3} and the chord ee joining its endpoints,

χe1+χe2+χe3−χe∈{0,2}.\chi_{e_{1}}+\chi_{e_{2}}+\chi_{e_{3}}-\chi_{e}\in\{0,2\}. (4.4)

Indeed, if χe=0\chi_{e}=0, then the endpoints of the path have the same sign, so χe1+χe2+χe3∈{0,2}\chi_{e_{1}}+\chi_{e_{2}}+\chi_{e_{3}}\in\{0,2\}. If χe=1\chi_{e}=1, then the endpoints have opposite signs, so χe1+χe2+χe3∈{1,3}\chi_{e_{1}}+\chi_{e_{2}}+\chi_{e_{3}}\in\{1,3\}. Hence, in either case, (4.4) holds.

If a chord has weight −w-w, w>0w>0, then

−wχe=−w∑f∈P⁡(e)χf+w(∑f∈P⁡(e)χf−χe),-w\chi_{e}=-w\sum_{f\in P(e)}\chi_{f}+w\left(\sum_{f\in P(e)}\chi_{f}-\chi_{e}\right), (4.5)

where P⁡(e)P(e) is the path joining its endpoints. The second term is nonnegative by (4.4). Thus the contribution −w​χe-w\chi_{e} of the negative chord can be rewritten by subtracting ww from the weight of each short edge in P⁡(e)P(e), together with the separate nonnegative correction w⁡(∑f∈P⁡(e)χf−χe)w\left(\sum_{f\in P(e)}\chi_{f}-\chi_{e}\right).

Lemma 4.2.

For cuts separating the endpoints of a single path,

min⁡cut𝖧j​(c)={c−3,j≥2,c≥3,c−1,j=1,c≥1.\min\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}=\begin{cases}c-3,&j\geq 2,\ c\geq 3,\\ c-1,&j=1,\ c\geq 1.\end{cases}

In particular, cut𝖧j​(c)−h⁡(𝖧j​(c))≥−2\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}-h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c))\geq-2 when j≥2j\geq 2 and c≥3c\geq 3.

Proof.

Apply the above chord replacement to all negative 33-chords in 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c). By Lemma 4.1, the weight of each SS-edge is reduced once, whereas the weight of each II-edge is reduced twice. Hence the resulting short-edge weights are respectively c−1c-1 and c−3c-3.

Any cut separating the two endpoints crosses at least one short edge. Hence, if j≥2j\geq 2 and c≥3c\geq 3, cut𝖧j​(c)≥c−3\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}\geq c-3. To attain this bound, choose a type I edge and assign one sign to all positions before it and the opposite sign to all positions after it. Then exactly this short edge crosses the cut. Moreover, each such path contains at most one sign change, so for every chord ee, ∑f∈P⁡(e)χf=χe\sum_{f\in P(e)}\chi_{f}=\chi_{e}. Thus all correction terms in (4.5) vanish, and the cut weight is exactly c−3c-3.

If j=1j=1, there are no type I edges, and every modified short edge has weight c−1c-1. Hence every endpoint-separating cut has weight at least c−1c-1. Isolating either endpoint crosses exactly one short edge and makes the correction term vanish, so the minimum is c−1c-1.

Finally, by (3.3), h⁡(𝖧j​(c))=c−1h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c))=c-1, and therefore, for j≥2j\geq 2, cut𝖧j​(c)−h⁡(𝖧j​(c))≥(c−3)−(c−1)=−2\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}-h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c))\geq(c-3)-(c-1)=-2. ∎

4.2 The product of two paths

For 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}, reverse the row indices in each coordinate and write the row and column vertices as

ru,v(0≤u≤j, 0≤v≤k),cx,y(0≤x≤j, 0≤y≤k),r_{u,v}\quad(0\leq u\leq j,\ 0\leq v\leq k),\qquad c_{x,y}\quad(0\leq x\leq j,\ 0\leq y\leq k),

where uu and xx are the fast coordinates, in accordance with the ordering convention introduced in Section 2. Thus ru,vr_{u,v} corresponds to the original row (j−u,k−v)(j-u,k-v), while cx,yc_{x,y} corresponds to column (x,y)(x,y). The corresponding entry of 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} is (𝖯k⊗𝖯j)(j−u,k−v),(x,y)=(𝖯k)k−v,y​(𝖯j)j−u,x(\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j})_{(j-u,k-v),(x,y)}=(\mathsf{P}_{k})_{k-v,y}(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{j-u,x}. Hence it is nonzero precisely when (𝖯j)j−u,x≠0(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{j-u,x}\neq 0 and (𝖯k)k−v,y≠0(\mathsf{P}_{k})_{k-v,y}\neq 0. By  (3.1), these conditions are equivalent to x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\} and y∈{v−1,v}y\in\{v-1,v\}, respectively. Let Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} be the corresponding bipartite graph, whose two parts consist of the row vertices and the column vertices, respectively. A row vertex ru,vr_{u,v} is adjacent to a column vertex cx,yc_{x,y} if and only if the corresponding entry of 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} is nonzero. By the calculation above, its adjacency rule is

ru,v∼cx,y⟺x∈{u−1,u},y∈{v−1,v},r_{u,v}\sim c_{x,y}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in\{u-1,u\},\quad y\in\{v-1,v\}, (4.6)

with indices outside their ranges discarded. The terminals are r0,0r_{0,0} and cj,kc_{j,k}, corresponding to the last row and the last column of 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}, respectively.

By the definition of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, if ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y} is an edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, then the corresponding entry of 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} is nonzero. Hence (𝖯j)j−u,x≠0(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{j-u,x}\neq 0 and (𝖯k)k−v,y≠0(\mathsf{P}_{k})_{k-v,y}\neq 0. Under the path representations of 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} and 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}, these two nonzero entries correspond to short edges of the respective paths. If these short edges are of types AA and BB, respectively, then ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y} is called an A​BAB-edge. Thus the possible types are S​SSS, S​ISI, I​SIS, and I​III, where the first letter records the type of the short edge corresponding to (𝖯j)j−u,x(\mathsf{P}_{j})_{j-u,x}, and the second records the type of the short edge corresponding to (𝖯k)k−v,y(\mathsf{P}_{k})_{k-v,y}.

Lemma 4.3.

For j,k≥1j,k\geq 1, the graph Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} is connected and its only bridges are

r0,0​c0,0andrj,k​cj,k.r_{0,0}c_{0,0}\quad\text{and}\quad r_{j,k}c_{j,k}. (4.7)

Consequently, every nonterminal cut separating the terminals crosses at least two edges of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}.

Proof.

We first show that Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} is connected. If 0≤u<j0\leq u<j, then by (4.6), ru,v∼cu,v∼ru+1,vr_{u,v}\sim c_{u,v}\sim r_{u+1,v}, so ru,vr_{u,v} and ru+1,vr_{u+1,v} are joined through cu,vc_{u,v}.

Similarly, if 0≤v<k0\leq v<k, then ru,v∼cu,v∼ru,v+1r_{u,v}\sim c_{u,v}\sim r_{u,v+1}, so ru,vr_{u,v} and ru,v+1r_{u,v+1} are joined through cu,vc_{u,v}.

Starting from r0,0r_{0,0} and repeatedly using these two types of connections, we can reach every row vertex ru,vr_{u,v}. Hence all row vertices lie in the same connected component.

For every column vertex cx,yc_{x,y}, the adjacency rule (4.6) gives cx,y∼rx,yc_{x,y}\sim r_{x,y}. Since all row vertices lie in the same connected component, so does every column vertex. Hence Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} is connected.

Consider an edge ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y}. Suppose first that x<jx<j and v>0v>0. By (4.6), x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\} and y∈{v−1,v}y\in\{v-1,v\}, or equivalently, u∈{x,x+1}u\in\{x,x+1\} and v∈{y,y+1}v\in\{y,y+1\}. Let u′u^{\prime} be the other member of {x,x+1}\{x,x+1\} besides uu, and let y′y^{\prime} be the other member of {v−1,v}\{v-1,v\} besides yy. We claim that

ru,v,cx,y,ru′,v,cx,y′,ru,vr_{u,v},\ c_{x,y},\ r_{u^{\prime},v},\ c_{x,y^{\prime}},\ r_{u,v}

is a four-cycle. The first edge is the original one. Taking cx,yc_{x,y} as the column vertex, the conditions u′∈{x,x+1}u^{\prime}\in\{x,x+1\} and v∈{y,y+1}v\in\{y,y+1\} hold by the definition of u′u^{\prime} and the original adjacency, so cx,y∼ru′,vc_{x,y}\sim r_{u^{\prime},v}. Next, x∈{u′−1,u′}x\in\{u^{\prime}-1,u^{\prime}\} and y′∈{v−1,v}y^{\prime}\in\{v-1,v\}, so ru′,v∼cx,y′r_{u^{\prime},v}\sim c_{x,y^{\prime}}. Finally, u∈{x,x+1}u\in\{x,x+1\} and v∈{y′,y′+1}v\in\{y^{\prime},y^{\prime}+1\}, and hence cx,y′∼ru,vc_{x,y^{\prime}}\sim r_{u,v}. Thus the displayed vertices form a four-cycle containing the original edge.

If y<ky<k and u>0u>0, interchange the two coordinates in this construction. When both conditions fail, the adjacency rule forces the edge to be one of (4.7). The two terminal vertices have degree one, so those edges are indeed bridges. Finally, a cut with just one crossing edge in a connected graph crosses a bridge. Here it must isolate one of the degree-one terminals, and is therefore a terminal cut. ∎

Lemma 4.4.

Throughout this lemma, the cuts under consideration separate the two terminals of the corresponding Kronecker product. If j,k≥1j,k\geq 1, then

𝒬⁡(𝖯j,𝖯k)≥0.\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{P}_{j},\mathsf{P}_{k})\geq 0. (4.8)

Also, 𝒬⁡(𝖯j,𝖧k​(d))≥0\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{P}_{j},\mathsf{H}_{k}(d))\geq 0 if either k=1,d≥4k=1,d\geq 4, or k≥2,d≥5k\geq 2,d\geq 5. The same statement holds with the factors interchanged.

Proof.

We first consider 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}. The nonzero entries of 𝖯k⊗𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} are all equal to 11, and its corresponding bipartite graph is Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}. By Lemma 4.3, Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} is connected. Hence every cut separating the two terminals crosses at least one edge, and therefore cut𝖯k⊗𝖯j≥1=h⁡(𝖯j)​h​(𝖯k)\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{P}_{k}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}}\geq 1=h(\mathsf{P}_{j})h(\mathsf{P}_{k}). This proves (4.8).

We next consider 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}. By Lemma 4.1, 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) has the same short-edge positions as 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}, with modified short-edge weights, together with 33-chords of weight −1-1. Hence the edges arising from the short-edge positions of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) and 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} still form the bipartite graph Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, with modified weights. The remaining edges arise from the 33-chord positions of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), together with nonzero entries of the 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j}-factor.

We next characterise the edges of 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} whose 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)-factor corresponds to a 33-chord of weight −1-1. By Lemma 4.1, in 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), the 33-chords of weight −1-1 correspond to matrix positions whose row and column indices sum to k+1k+1. In the coordinates of Section 4.2, the 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)-row index corresponding to ru,vr_{u,v} is k−vk-v. Thus (k−v)+y=k+1(k-v)+y=k+1 if and only if y=v+1y=v+1. On the other hand, the 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j}-factor is nonzero precisely when x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\}. Consequently, the edges arising from these 33-chords, and only these edges, have the form

ru,v​cx,v+1,x∈{u−1,u},0≤v≤k−1,r_{u,v}c_{x,v+1},\qquad x\in\{u-1,u\},\qquad 0\leq v\leq k-1,

with indices outside their ranges discarded.

Fix one of these edges. We claim that

ru,v−cx,v−ru,v+1−cx,v+1r_{u,v}-c_{x,v}-r_{u,v+1}-c_{x,v+1}

is a path joining the same two endpoints. Indeed, since x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\}, equation (4.6) gives ru,v∼cx,vr_{u,v}\sim c_{x,v}. Also, u∈{x,x+1}u\in\{x,x+1\} and v+1∈{v,v+1}v+1\in\{v,v+1\}, so cx,v∼ru,v+1c_{x,v}\sim r_{u,v+1}. Finally, x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\} and v+1∈{v,v+1}v+1\in\{v,v+1\} give ru,v+1∼cx,v+1r_{u,v+1}\sim c_{x,v+1}. Thus this path has the same endpoints as the edge ru,v​cx,v+1r_{u,v}c_{x,v+1}. We call this the replacement path associated with ru,v​cx,v+1r_{u,v}c_{x,v+1}. Therefore (4.5), with w=1w=1, applies to this edge.

Apply this replacement to every such edge. In the sum of these identities, the weight of each edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} is reduced by one for each replacement path containing it. Thus it remains only to determine how many replacement paths contain each edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}.

Fix uu and x∈{u−1,u}x\in\{u-1,u\}. For 0≤t≤k−10\leq t\leq k-1, write

Rt:ru,t−cx,t−ru,t+1−cx,t+1.R_{t}:\qquad r_{u,t}-c_{x,t}-r_{u,t+1}-c_{x,t+1}.

Its three edges are

ru,t​cx,t,ru,t+1​cx,t,ru,t+1​cx,t+1.r_{u,t}c_{x,t},\qquad r_{u,t+1}c_{x,t},\qquad r_{u,t+1}c_{x,t+1}.

First consider

ru,v​cx,v−1,1≤v≤k.r_{u,v}c_{x,v-1},\qquad 1\leq v\leq k.

In the path representation of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), row k−vk-v is placed at position 2​v2v, while column v−1v-1 is placed at position 2​(v−1)+1=2​v−12(v-1)+1=2v-1. Thus the corresponding 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)-short edge is (2​v−1,2​v)(2v-1,2v), which is a type SS edge by Lemma 4.1. Moreover, ru,v​cx,v−1r_{u,v}c_{x,v-1} occurs exactly as the middle edge of Rv−1R_{v-1}, and it cannot occur in any other RtR_{t}. Hence every edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} of this form is used exactly once.

Next consider

ru,v​cx,v.r_{u,v}c_{x,v}.

For the edge ru,v​cx,vr_{u,v}c_{x,v}, the corresponding short edge in the path representation of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) is (2​v,2​v+1)(2v,2v+1). By Lemma 4.1, this is a type SS edge when v=0v=0 or v=kv=k, and a type II edge when 1≤v≤k−11\leq v\leq k-1.

If v=0v=0, the edge ru,0​cx,0r_{u,0}c_{x,0} occurs only as the first edge of R0R_{0}. If v=kv=k, the edge ru,k​cx,kr_{u,k}c_{x,k} occurs only as the last edge of Rk−1R_{k-1}. Thus these two boundary type SS edges are also used exactly once. Finally, if 1≤v≤k−11\leq v\leq k-1, then ru,v​cx,vr_{u,v}c_{x,v} is the first edge of RvR_{v} and the last edge of Rv−1R_{v-1}. It is not the middle edge of any replacement path.

Thus the above counting shows that every edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} corresponding to an SS-edge in the path representation of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) is used once, whereas every edge corresponding to an II-edge is used twice. Since the corresponding nonzero entry of 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} is 11, these edges have weights dd and d−1d-1, respectively, before the replacements. Hence their resulting weights are d−1d-1 and d−3d-3, respectively, and all correction terms arising from (4.5) are nonnegative.

Suppose first that k≥2k\geq 2. By Lemma 4.3, every nonterminal cut separating the two terminals crosses at least two edges of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}. Every remaining edge of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} has weight at least d−3d-3. Therefore, when d≥5d\geq 5, cut𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j≥2​(d−3)≥d−1\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}}\geq 2(d-3)\geq d-1 for every nonterminal cut. For either terminal cut, the cut sum is the last row or column sum of 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}. By the row-sum property of the Kronecker product and (3.3), cut𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j=h⁡(𝖯j)​h​(𝖧k​(d))=d−1\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}}=h(\mathsf{P}_{j})h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d))=d-1. Hence 𝒬⁡(𝖯j,𝖧k​(d))≥0\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{P}_{j},\mathsf{H}_{k}(d))\geq 0.

If k=1k=1, there are no type II short edges in 𝖧1​(d)\mathsf{H}_{1}(d). Thus every remaining edge of Γj,1\Gamma_{j,1} has weight d−1d-1. Since Γj,1\Gamma_{j,1} is connected by Lemma 4.3, every cut separating the terminals crosses at least one such edge. Therefore cut𝖧1​(d)⊗𝖯j≥d−1=h⁡(𝖯j)​h​(𝖧1​(d))\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{1}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j}}\geq d-1=h(\mathsf{P}_{j})h(\mathsf{H}_{1}(d)), and hence 𝒬⁡(𝖯j,𝖧1​(d))≥0\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{P}_{j},\mathsf{H}_{1}(d))\geq 0.

Finally, interchanging the two coordinates merely relabels the same weighted bipartite graph and preserves the two terminals. Therefore the same conclusion holds with the factors interchanged. ∎

We next need a more detailed count when the path representations of both factors contain 33-chords. Delete the type II edges from Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} and denote the resulting graph by Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}. Call the SI- and IS-edges mixed edges.

Lemma 4.5.

In the spanning subgraph of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k} consisting of the SS-edges, the connected components are indexed by (ρ,σ)∈{1,…,j}×{1,…,k}(\rho,\sigma)\in\{1,\ldots,j\}\times\{1,\ldots,k\}. We call these the SS-components. More precisely, define

λ⁡(ru,v)=(max⁡(1,u),max⁡(1,v)),λ⁡(cx,y)=(min⁡(j,x+1),min⁡(k,y+1)).\lambda(r_{u,v})=(\max(1,u),\max(1,v)),\qquad\lambda(c_{x,y})=(\min(j,x+1),\min(k,y+1)). (4.9)

Two vertices belong to the same SS-component if and only if they have the same label.

Proof.

For an edge ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y}, the corresponding short edge in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} is of type S precisely when either x=u−1x=u-1, or x=ux=u and u∈{0,j}u\in\{0,j\}. In either case, max⁡(1,u)=min⁡(j,x+1)\max(1,u)=\min(j,x+1).

Similarly, the corresponding short edge in 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k} is of type S precisely when either y=v−1y=v-1, or y=vy=v and v∈{0,k}v\in\{0,k\}. In either case, max⁡(1,v)=min⁡(k,y+1)\max(1,v)=\min(k,y+1). Therefore every SS-edge joins two vertices with the same label in (4.9).

Conversely, fix (ρ,σ)∈{1,…,j}×{1,…,k}(\rho,\sigma)\in\{1,\ldots,j\}\times\{1,\ldots,k\}. The row vertices with label (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) are exactly the vertices ru,vr_{u,v} for which

u={ρ,ρ>1,0​ or ​1,ρ=1,v={σ,σ>1,0​ or ​1,σ=1.u=\begin{cases}\rho,&\rho>1,\\ 0\text{ or }1,&\rho=1,\end{cases}\qquad v=\begin{cases}\sigma,&\sigma>1,\\ 0\text{ or }1,&\sigma=1.\end{cases}

Every such row vertex is joined by an SS-edge to cρ−1,σ−1c_{\rho-1,\sigma-1}.

Likewise, the column vertices with label (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) are exactly the vertices cx,yc_{x,y} for which

x={ρ−1,ρ<j,j−1​ or ​j,ρ=j,y={σ−1,σ<k,k−1​ or ​k,σ=k.x=\begin{cases}\rho-1,&\rho<j,\\ j-1\text{ or }j,&\rho=j,\end{cases}\qquad y=\begin{cases}\sigma-1,&\sigma<k,\\ k-1\text{ or }k,&\sigma=k.\end{cases}

Every such column vertex is joined by an SS-edge to rρ,σr_{\rho,\sigma}.

Since rρ,σ​cρ−1,σ−1r_{\rho,\sigma}c_{\rho-1,\sigma-1} is itself an SS-edge, all vertices with label (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) lie in the same SS-component. Together with the preceding paragraph, this shows that the SS-components are exactly the label classes in (4.9). ∎

Lemma 4.6.

After contracting the SS-components of Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}, the mixed edges form a rectangular grid on {1,…,j}×{1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,j\}\times\{1,\ldots,k\}, possibly with parallel edges. For 1≤ρ≤j1\leq\rho\leq j and 1≤σ≤k−11\leq\sigma\leq k-1, the number of SI-edges joining the SS-components labelled (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) and (ρ,σ+1)(\rho,\sigma+1) is

μj​(ρ)={3,j=1,2,j≥2,ρ∈{1,j},1,1<ρ<j.\mu_{j}(\rho)=\begin{cases}3,&j=1,\\ 2,&j\geq 2,\ \rho\in\{1,j\},\\ 1,&1<\rho<j.\end{cases} (4.10)

Similarly, for 1≤ρ≤j−11\leq\rho\leq j-1 and 1≤σ≤k1\leq\sigma\leq k, the number of IS-edges joining (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) and (ρ+1,σ)(\rho+1,\sigma) is μk​(σ)\mu_{k}(\sigma). In particular, Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k} is connected.

Proof.

Fix 1≤ρ≤j1\leq\rho\leq j and 1≤σ≤k−11\leq\sigma\leq k-1, and consider an SI-edge ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y} joining the SS-components labelled (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) and (ρ,σ+1)(\rho,\sigma+1). By (4.6) and Lemma 4.1, the short edge corresponding to the 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}-entry is of type I precisely when y=v=ty=v=t for some t∈{1,…,k−1}t\in\{1,\ldots,k-1\}. By (4.9), the second coordinates of the endpoint labels are then tt and t+1t+1, respectively. Hence t=σt=\sigma. Thus the corresponding I-edge in 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k} is fixed, and it remains only to count the possible pairs (u,x)(u,x) for which the corresponding short edge in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} is of type S and both endpoint labels have first coordinate ρ\rho.

If j≥2j\geq 2, these pairs are (ρ,ρ−1)(\rho,\rho-1), together with (0,0)(0,0) when ρ=1\rho=1 and (j,j)(j,j) when ρ=j\rho=j. Hence μj​(ρ)=2\mu_{j}(\rho)=2 for ρ∈{1,j}\rho\in\{1,j\} and μj​(ρ)=1\mu_{j}(\rho)=1 for 1<ρ<j1<\rho<j. If j=1j=1, the three possible pairs are (0,0)(0,0), (1,0)(1,0), and (1,1)(1,1), for all of which the endpoint labels have first coordinate 11, so μ1​(1)=3\mu_{1}(1)=3. This proves (4.10).

The IS-edges are counted in the same way after interchanging the roles of jj and kk. Hence the number joining (ρ,σ)(\rho,\sigma) and (ρ+1,σ)(\rho+1,\sigma) is μk​(σ)\mu_{k}(\sigma).

Thus every pair of horizontally or vertically adjacent labels is joined by at least one mixed edge. Conversely, by (4.6) and (4.9), every mixed edge joins two labels that agree in one coordinate and differ by one in the other. After contracting the SS-components, the underlying simple graph is therefore the rectangular grid on {1,…,j}×{1,…,k}\{1,\ldots,j\}\times\{1,\ldots,k\}, and hence is connected. Since each contracted vertex represents a connected SS-component, it follows that Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k} itself is connected. ∎

Lemma 4.7.

Among the type SS edges of Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}, the only bridges are the two terminal edges

r0,0​c0,0,rj,k​cj,k.r_{0,0}c_{0,0},\qquad r_{j,k}c_{j,k}.
Proof.

If j=1j=1, then 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} has no type I edges, while if k=1k=1, then 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k} has no type I edges. Hence, if j=1j=1 or k=1k=1, there are no type II edges in Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, and therefore Γj,k′=Γj,k\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}=\Gamma_{j,k}. The result then follows from Lemma 4.3. Thus we may assume j,k≥2j,k\geq 2.

For an edge ru,v​cx,yr_{u,v}c_{x,y} of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, the corresponding short edge in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} is of type S precisely when x=u−1x=u-1, or when x=ux=u with u∈{0,j}u\in\{0,j\}; similarly, the corresponding short edge in 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k} is of type S precisely when y=v−1y=v-1, or when y=vy=v with v∈{0,k}v\in\{0,k\}. We call the type S edges arising from x=ux=u with u∈{0,j}u\in\{0,j\} in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j}, and from y=vy=v with v∈{0,k}v\in\{0,k\} in 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}, the boundary S edges.

For 1≤u≤j1\leq u\leq j and 1≤v≤k1\leq v\leq k, we call ru,v​cu−1,v−1r_{u,v}c_{u-1,v-1} the core SS-edge of the component labelled (u,v)(u,v). All other type SS edges will be referred to as noncore SS-edges.

We first consider the core SS-edges. If u≥2u\geq 2 and v≤k−1v\leq k-1, this edge lies on the six-cycle

ru,v,cu−1,v,ru−1,v+1,cu−2,v,ru−1,v,cu−1,v−1,ru,v.r_{u,v},\ c_{u-1,v},\ r_{u-1,v+1},\ c_{u-2,v},\ r_{u-1,v},\ c_{u-1,v-1},\ r_{u,v}.

Each consecutive pair satisfies (4.6); the six edge types are, in order, S​I,I​S,S​S,S​I,I​S,S​SSI,IS,SS,SI,IS,SS. Hence the entire cycle lies in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}. If instead u≤j−1u\leq j-1 and v≥2v\geq 2, the core edge lies on

ru,v,cu,v−1,ru+1,v−1,cu,v−2,ru,v−1,cu−1,v−1,ru,v,r_{u,v},\ c_{u,v-1},\ r_{u+1,v-1},\ c_{u,v-2},\ r_{u,v-1},\ c_{u-1,v-1},\ r_{u,v},

whose edge types are I​S,S​I,S​S,I​S,S​I,S​SIS,SI,SS,IS,SI,SS. Again the whole cycle is contained in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}. These two cases cover all core labels except (1,1)(1,1) and (j,k)(j,k). The two remaining core edges lie, respectively, on the four-cycles

r1,1,c0,0,r0,1,c0,1,r1,1,\displaystyle r_{1,1},\ c_{0,0},\ r_{0,1},\ c_{0,1},\ r_{1,1},
rj,k,cj−1,k−1,rj,k−1,cj,k−1,rj,k.\displaystyle r_{j,k},\ c_{j-1,k-1},\ r_{j,k-1},\ c_{j,k-1},\ r_{j,k}.

Every consecutive pair in these cycles satisfies (4.6), and every edge has at most one type I coordinate. Thus both cycles lie in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}. Consequently, no core SS-edge is a bridge.

It remains to consider the noncore SS-edges. By the preceding classification of type S edges in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} and 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}, every noncore type SS edge uses a boundary type S edge in at least one of the two factors. Hence the noncore type SS edges consist of the four families

r0,v​c0,v−1,\displaystyle r_{0,v}c_{0,v-1}, 1≤v≤k,\displaystyle 1\leq v\leq k,
rj,v​cj,v−1,\displaystyle r_{j,v}c_{j,v-1}, 1≤v≤k,\displaystyle 1\leq v\leq k,

ru,k​cu−1,k,\displaystyle r_{u,k}c_{u-1,k}, 1≤u≤j,\displaystyle 1\leq u\leq j,

together with the four corner edges r0,0​c0,0r_{0,0}c_{0,0}, r0,k​c0,kr_{0,k}c_{0,k}, rj,0​cj,0r_{j,0}c_{j,0}, and rj,k​cj,kr_{j,k}c_{j,k}.

Each edge in the first family lies on the four-cycle

By (4.6), all four adjacencies hold. Moreover, the short edge in 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} corresponding to each edge of this cycle is of type S, so none of its edges is of type II. Hence the cycle lies in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}.

The other three families are treated in the same way, using the four-cycles

rj,v−cj,v−1−rj,v−1−cj−1,v−1−rj,v,\displaystyle r_{j,v}-c_{j,v-1}-r_{j,v-1}-c_{j-1,v-1}-r_{j,v}, 1≤v≤k,\displaystyle 1\leq v\leq k,
ru,0−cu−1,0−ru,1−cu,0−ru,0,\displaystyle r_{u,0}-c_{u-1,0}-r_{u,1}-c_{u,0}-r_{u,0}, 1≤u≤j,\displaystyle 1\leq u\leq j,
ru,k−cu−1,k−ru−1,k−cu−1,k−1−ru,k,\displaystyle r_{u,k}-c_{u-1,k}-r_{u-1,k}-c_{u-1,k-1}-r_{u,k}, 1≤u≤j.\displaystyle 1\leq u\leq j.

Thus every edge in the four families lies on a cycle in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}.

These cycles also contain the two nonterminal corner edges r0,k​c0,kr_{0,k}c_{0,k} and rj,0​cj,0r_{j,0}c_{j,0}. Therefore the only noncore type SS edges not yet shown to lie on a cycle are r0,0​c0,0r_{0,0}c_{0,0} and rj,k​cj,kr_{j,k}c_{j,k}. By (4.6), r0,0r_{0,0} and cj,kc_{j,k} both have degree one. Hence these two edges are bridges, completing the proof. ∎

4.3 Two factors with negative 3-chords

The following is the estimate that will be used in the transform decomposition.

Theorem 4.8.

Let each of A,DA,D be one of the matrices

𝖯j​(j≥1),𝖧1​(c)​(c≥4),𝖧j​(c)​(j≥2,c≥5).\mathsf{P}_{j}\ (j\geq 1),\qquad\mathsf{H}_{1}(c)\ (c\geq 4),\qquad\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)\ (j\geq 2,\ c\geq 5).

Every cut separating the terminals of D⊗AD\otimes A satisfies

cutD⊗A≥h⁡(A)​h​(D).\operatorname{cut}_{D\otimes A}\geq h(A)h(D). (4.11)

If both factors are H matrices, equality holds only for the two terminal cuts. Furthermore, if j,k≥2j,k\geq 2 and c,d≥5c,d\geq 5, every nonterminal cut separating the terminals satisfies

cut𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖧j​(c)−(c−1)​(d−1)≥5.\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}-(c-1)(d-1)\geq 5. (4.12)
Proof.

The cases 𝖯j⊗𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{j}\otimes\mathsf{P}_{k}, 𝖯j⊗𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{P}_{j}\otimes\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), and 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} are covered by Lemma 4.4. We therefore consider 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c).

We use the same row and column indexing as in Section 4.2. By Lemma 4.1, 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) and 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) have the same short-edge positions as 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j} and 𝖯k\mathsf{P}_{k}, respectively. Hence the edges corresponding to the short-edge positions in both factors still form the bipartite graph Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, with modified weights.

Now consider an edge for which a 33-chord position occurs in exactly one of the two factors. Suppose first that the 33-chord position lies in 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), while the position in 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) is a short-edge position. Since the short-edge positions of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) are exactly the nonzero positions of 𝖯j\mathsf{P}_{j}, these negative edges and their replacement paths occur in exactly the same positions as those already obtained for 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} in Lemma 4.4.

More precisely, such a negative edge has the form

ru,v​cx,v+1,x∈{u−1,u},0≤v≤k−1,r_{u,v}c_{x,v+1},\qquad x\in\{u-1,u\},\qquad 0\leq v\leq k-1,

and its replacement path is

ru,v−cx,v−ru,v+1−cx,v+1.r_{u,v}-c_{x,v}-r_{u,v+1}-c_{x,v+1}.

The only difference from the 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} case is the weight. If the corresponding short edge of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) has weight α\alpha, then the negative edge has weight −α-\alpha, and (4.5) is applied to the same replacement path with w=αw=\alpha.

Similarly, after interchanging the two factors, if the 33-chord position lies in 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) while the position in 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) is a short-edge position, then the corresponding negative edges and replacement paths are obtained in the same way. Such a negative edge has the form

ru,v​cu+1,y,0≤u≤j−1,y∈{v−1,v},r_{u,v}c_{u+1,y},\qquad 0\leq u\leq j-1,\qquad y\in\{v-1,v\},

with replacement path

ru,v−cu,y−ru+1,v−cu+1,y.r_{u,v}-c_{u,y}-r_{u+1,v}-c_{u+1,y}.

If the short edge of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) corresponding to the position (k−v,y)(k-v,y) has weight β\beta, then the negative edge has weight −β-\beta, and (4.5) is applied with w=βw=\beta.

Finally, if the corresponding positions in both factors are 33-chord positions, then the resulting edge has weight (−1)​(−1)=1(-1)(-1)=1.

Apply the above replacements to all negative edges, and fix an edge f=ru,v​cx,yf=r_{u,v}c_{x,y} of Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}.

Consider first the replacements arising from 33-chord positions of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d). As observed above, their replacement paths are exactly the same as those in the 𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{P}_{j} case of Lemma 4.4. Hence, by the counting already carried out there, ff is contained in exactly one such replacement path if its corresponding short edge in the path representation of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) is of type S, and in exactly two if that short edge is of type I.

Similarly, after interchanging the two factors, the same counting rule holds for the short edge of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) corresponding to ff.

Let α\alpha and β\beta be the weights of the short edges corresponding to ff in the path representations of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) and 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d), respectively. Define

m1\displaystyle m_{1} ={1,if the corresponding short edge of 𝖧j​(c) is of type S,2,if it is of type I,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if the corresponding short edge of $\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)$ is of type~S},\\ 2,&\text{if it is of type~I},\end{cases}
m2\displaystyle m_{2} ={1,if the corresponding short edge of 𝖧k​(d) is of type S,2,if it is of type I.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}1,&\text{if the corresponding short edge of $\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)$ is of type~S},\\ 2,&\text{if it is of type~I}.\end{cases}

For a replacement arising from a 33-chord in one factor, the corresponding matrix position in the other factor is the same for all three edges of the replacement path.

Before the replacements, the weight of ff is α​β\alpha\beta. Each replacement arising from a 33-chord of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c) reduces the weight of ff by β\beta, and there are m1m_{1} such replacements containing ff. Likewise, each replacement arising from a 33-chord of 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d) reduces the weight of ff by α\alpha, and there are m2m_{2} such replacements containing ff. Therefore the remaining weight of ff is

α​β−m1​β−m2​α.\alpha\beta-m_{1}\beta-m_{2}\alpha. (4.13)

Apply (4.5) to every negative edge and sum the resulting exact identities. Let RR be the weighted graph with underlying graph Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, whose edge weights are the remaining weights given by (4.13). Then

cut𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖧j​(c)=cutR+∑e​ positiveχe+∑e​ negative|we|​(∑f∈P⁡(e)χf−χe).\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}=\operatorname{cut}_{R}+\sum_{e\text{ positive}}\chi_{e}+\sum_{e\text{ negative}}|w_{e}|\left(\sum_{f\in P(e)}\chi_{f}-\chi_{e}\right). (4.14)

For each negative edge ee, wew_{e} denotes its original weight and P⁡(e)P(e) is its associated replacement path. Here the first sum is over the positive edges whose corresponding positions in both factors are 33-chord positions; each such edge has weight one. Each correction term in the second sum is nonnegative by (4.4). Hence cut𝖧k​(d)⊗𝖧j​(c)≥cutR\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)}\geq\operatorname{cut}_{R}. We first treat the three minimal parameter cases.

Both indices at least two: j,k≥2j,k\geq 2 and c=d=5c=d=5. By (4.13), the edge weights in RR are

typeSSSI​ or ​ISIIweight25−5−5=1520−10−4=616−8−8=0.\begin{array}[]{c|ccc}\text{type}&\mathrm{SS}&\mathrm{SI}\text{ or }\mathrm{IS}&\mathrm{II}\\ \hline\cr\text{weight}&25-5-5=15&20-10-4=6&16-8-8=0.\end{array}

In this case, h⁡(𝖧j​(5))​h​(𝖧k​(5))=(5−1)2=16h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(5))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(5))=(5-1)^{2}=16, so it remains to prove that every terminal-separating cut has weight at least 1616.

For nonterminal cuts, the contributions of the SS-edges and the mixed edges of RR suffice for the required lower bound, so we restrict attention to these edges. Since the underlying graph of RR is Γj,k\Gamma_{j,k}, the SS-edges and the mixed edges of RR form precisely Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}.

If a cut crosses at least two SS-edges, its weight in RR is at least 3030. If it crosses an SS-edge and a mixed edge, the weight is at least 15+6=2115+6=21. If it crosses exactly one SS-edge and no mixed edge, that edge is the only edge of Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k} crossing the cut. By Lemma 4.6, this graph is connected, so the edge is a bridge. Lemma 4.7 then shows that this is a terminal cut.

Now suppose no SS-edge crosses the cut. Then each SS-component lies entirely on one side of the cut, so these components may be contracted without losing information about the separation of the two terminals. Hence it remains only to count mixed SI/IS edges between distinct SS-components.

By Lemma 4.6, after contracting the SS-components, the mixed edges form a rectangular grid on the component labels. The terminal components have labels (1,1)(1,1) and (j,k)(j,k), and these labels carry opposite signs. Consider the two boundary paths

(1,1),(2,1),…,(j,1),(j,2),…,(j,k)(1,1),(2,1),\ldots,(j,1),(j,2),\ldots,(j,k)

and

(1,1),(1,2),…,(1,k),(2,k),…,(j,k).(1,1),(1,2),\ldots,(1,k),(2,k),\ldots,(j,k).

The two paths are edge-disjoint, and each has endpoints of opposite signs. Hence each path contains a pair of adjacent labels with opposite signs, giving two distinct such boundary pairs. By (4.10), each of these boundary pairs is joined by exactly two mixed edges in Γj,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{j,k}. Therefore at least four mixed edges cross the original cut, and hence cutR≥4⋅6=24\operatorname{cut}_{R}\geq 4\cdot 6=24.

Together with (4.14), these estimates show that every nonterminal cut of 𝖧k​(5)⊗𝖧j​(5)\mathsf{H}_{k}(5)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(5) has weight at least 21=16+521=16+5. A terminal cut of this Kronecker product has weight h⁡(𝖧j​(5))​h​(𝖧k​(5))=16h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(5))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(5))=16 by (3.3). This proves both the equality assertion and (4.12) at (c,d)=(5,5)(c,d)=(5,5).

One index equals one: j=1,k≥2j=1,k\geq 2 and c=4,d=5c=4,d=5. By Lemma 4.1, 𝖧1​(4)\mathsf{H}_{1}(4) has no type II short edge. Hence every edge of RR is of type S​SSS or S​ISI. By (4.13), their weights are respectively 4⋅5−5−4=114\cdot 5-5-4=11 and 4⋅4−4−8=44\cdot 4-4-8=4. In this case, h⁡(𝖧1​(4))​h​(𝖧k​(5))=(4−1)​(5−1)=12h(\mathsf{H}_{1}(4))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(5))=(4-1)(5-1)=12, so it remains to prove that every terminal-separating cut has weight at least 1212.

Since the underlying graph of RR is Γ1,k\Gamma_{1,k}, its S​SSS-edges and mixed edges form precisely Γ1,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{1,k}.

If a cut crosses at least two S​SSS-edges, then its weight in RR is at least 2⋅11=222\cdot 11=22. If it crosses an S​SSS-edge together with a mixed edge, then its weight in RR is at least 11+4=1511+4=15. If it crosses exactly one S​SSS-edge and no mixed edge, then that edge is the only edge of Γ1,k′\Gamma^{\prime}_{1,k} crossing the cut; by Lemmas 4.6 and 4.7, the cut is terminal.

Now suppose that no S​SSS-edge crosses the cut. Since j=1j=1, the contracted rectangular grid of Lemma 4.6 reduces to the path (1,1),(1,2),…,(1,k)(1,1),(1,2),\ldots,(1,k). The two endpoint labels represent the SS-components containing the terminals and therefore have opposite signs; hence at least one sign change occurs along this path. By (4.10), each pair of consecutive labels is joined by three mixed edges. Hence, if there are at least two sign changes along this path, then cutR≥2⋅3⋅4=24\operatorname{cut}_{R}\geq 2\cdot 3\cdot 4=24.

It remains to consider the case of exactly one sign change, say between (1,h)(1,h) and (1,h+1)(1,h+1), where 1≤h<k1\leq h<k. The three mixed edges joining these two labels contribute 3⋅4=123\cdot 4=12 to cutR\operatorname{cut}_{R}.

To obtain strict inequality in this remaining case, consider the edge r0,h−1​c1,hr_{0,h-1}c_{1,h}. Here the column coordinates satisfy 1=0+11=0+1 and h=(h−1)+1h=(h-1)+1. By the characterisation of the 33-chord positions above, the corresponding positions in both 𝖧1​(4)\mathsf{H}_{1}(4) and 𝖧k​(5)\mathsf{H}_{k}(5) are 33-chord positions. Hence this is one of the additional positive edges appearing in the first sum of (4.14), and it has weight one.

By the label formulas in (4.9), its endpoints belong to the S​SSS-components labelled (1,max⁡{1,h−1})(1,\max\{1,h-1\}) and (1,h+1)(1,h+1). Because the unique sign change occurs between hh and h+1h+1, and max⁡{1,h−1}≤h\max\{1,h-1\}\leq h, these two components have opposite signs. Thus this additional positive edge also crosses the cut. Together with the three mixed edges above,

cut𝖧k​(5)⊗𝖧1​(4)≥12+1=13>12.\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(5)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{1}(4)}\geq 12+1=13>12.

Terminal cuts have weight h⁡(𝖧1​(4))​h​(𝖧k​(5))=12h(\mathsf{H}_{1}(4))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(5))=12 by (3.3). The case k=1,j≥2k=1,j\geq 2 follows by interchanging the two coordinates.

Both indices equal one: j=k=1j=k=1 and c=d=4c=d=4. By Lemma 4.1, in the path representations of both factors, every short edge is of type SS. Hence every edge of RR is of type S​SSS, and by (4.13) its weight is 4⋅4−4−4=84\cdot 4-4-4=8. In this case, h​(𝖧1​(4))2=(4−1)2=9h(\mathsf{H}_{1}(4))^{2}=(4-1)^{2}=9, so it remains to prove that every terminal-separating cut has weight at least 99.

Since the underlying graph of RR is Γ1,1\Gamma_{1,1}, Lemma 4.3 implies that every nonterminal cut separating the two terminals crosses at least two edges of RR. Therefore cutR≥2⋅8=16>9\operatorname{cut}_{R}\geq 2\cdot 8=16>9. By (4.14), the weight of the corresponding cut of 𝖧1​(4)⊗𝖧1​(4)\mathsf{H}_{1}(4)\otimes\mathsf{H}_{1}(4) is at least cutR\operatorname{cut}_{R}. Hence every nonterminal cut has weight strictly greater than 99, whereas the terminal cuts have weight h​(𝖧1​(4))2=9h(\mathsf{H}_{1}(4))^{2}=9 by (3.3).

To pass from the minimal admissible parameters to arbitrary cc and dd, let c0=4c_{0}=4 if j=1j=1 and c0=5c_{0}=5 otherwise, and define d0d_{0} in the same way. By the definition of 𝖧j​(c)\mathsf{H}_{j}(c), 𝖧j​(c)=𝖧j​(c0)+(c−c0)​𝖯j\mathsf{H}_{j}(c)=\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{0})+(c-c_{0})\mathsf{P}_{j}, and similarly for 𝖧k​(d)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d). Since 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is bilinear in its matrix arguments for each fixed cut by (3.7),

𝒬⁡(𝖧j​(c),𝖧k​(d))=\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c),\mathsf{H}_{k}(d))={} 𝒬⁡(𝖧j​(c0),𝖧k​(d0))\displaystyle\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{0}),\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{0})) (4.15)
+(c−c0)​𝒬​(𝖯j,𝖧k​(d0))\displaystyle+(c-c_{0})\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{P}_{j},\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{0}))
+(d−d0)​𝒬​(𝖧j​(c0),𝖯k)\displaystyle+(d-d_{0})\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{0}),\mathsf{P}_{k})

Here c−c0,d−d0≥0c-c_{0},d-d_{0}\geq 0, and the last three terms are nonnegative by Lemma 4.4. On the other hand, terminal cuts have 𝒬=0\mathcal{Q}=0 for all parameters by (3.3). Therefore equality in (4.11) holds exactly for the terminal cuts. When j,k≥2j,k\geq 2, the base-case bound 𝒬⁡(𝖧j​(5),𝖧k​(5))≥5\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(5),\mathsf{H}_{k}(5))\geq 5 is preserved by (4.15), proving (4.12). This proves all assertions. ∎

5 The two maximising divisor sets

We now apply Theorem 4.8 to the decomposition of 𝖡a​(p)\mathsf{B}_{a}(p) and 𝖡b​(q)\mathsf{B}_{b}(q). Odd exponents give only H matrices. Even exponents also give a last-coordinate term, whose possible loss will be bounded using Lemma 4.2.

Proposition 5.1.

Let a,ba,b be positive odd integers and let p,q≥5p,q\geq 5 be real. Every cut separating the last row and column vertices of 𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p) has weight at least ga​(p)​gb​(q)g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q). Equality holds exactly at the two terminal cuts.

Proof.

Since aa and bb are odd, (3.5) gives

𝖡a​(p)\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{a}(p) =∑j=a,a−2,…j≥3pj−2​(p−1)​𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(p))+𝒥a,1​(𝖧1​(p−1)),\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=a,a-2,\ldots\\ j\geq 3\end{subarray}}p^{j-2}(p-1)\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(p))+\mathcal{J}_{a,1}(\mathsf{H}_{1}(p-1)),
𝖡b​(q)\displaystyle\mathsf{B}_{b}(q) =∑k=b,b−2,…k≥3qk−2​(q−1)​𝒥b,k​(𝖧k​(q))+𝒥b,1​(𝖧1​(q−1)).\displaystyle=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=b,b-2,\ldots\\ k\geq 3\end{subarray}}q^{k-2}(q-1)\mathcal{J}_{b,k}(\mathsf{H}_{k}(q))+\mathcal{J}_{b,1}(\mathsf{H}_{1}(q-1)).

For the indices occurring above, write

cj={p,j≥3,p−1,j=1,dk={q,k≥3,q−1,k=1,αj={pj−2​(p−1),j≥3,1,j=1,βk={qk−2​(q−1),k≥3,1,k=1.\begin{gathered}c_{j}=\begin{cases}p,&j\geq 3,\\ p-1,&j=1,\end{cases}\qquad d_{k}=\begin{cases}q,&k\geq 3,\\ q-1,&k=1,\end{cases}\\ \alpha_{j}=\begin{cases}p^{j-2}(p-1),&j\geq 3,\\ 1,&j=1,\end{cases}\qquad\beta_{k}=\begin{cases}q^{k-2}(q-1),&k\geq 3,\\ 1,&k=1.\end{cases}\end{gathered}

All these coefficients are positive. Moreover, for j≥3j\geq 3 the corresponding factor is 𝖧j​(p)\mathsf{H}_{j}(p) with p≥5p\geq 5, whereas for j=1j=1 it is 𝖧1​(p−1)\mathsf{H}_{1}(p-1) with p−1≥4p-1\geq 4; the same statements hold on the qq-side. Thus every pair of H factors occurring in the two decompositions satisfies the parameter assumptions of Theorem 4.8.

Fix a cut separating the last row and column vertices of 𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p). For a pair of indices j,kj,k, the matrices 𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(cj))\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})) and 𝒥b,k​(𝖧k​(dk))\mathcal{J}_{b,k}(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})) are supported on the coordinate sets {a−j,…,a}\{a-j,\ldots,a\} and {b−k,…,b}\{b-k,\ldots,b\}, respectively. Hence, in the original row and column coordinates, their tensor product is supported on the lower-right rectangle {a−j,…,a}×{b−k,…,b}\{a-j,\ldots,a\}\times\{b-k,\ldots,b\}. This rectangle contains the final coordinate (a,b)(a,b), so its last row and column vertices are precisely the two global terminals. Therefore the restriction of the fixed global cut to this rectangle still separates the two terminals.

The embedded tensor product differs from 𝖧k​(dk)⊗𝖧j​(cj)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}) only by zero rows and columns outside this lower-right rectangle, and these zero entries make no contribution to the cut weight. When the fixed global cut is restricted to this rectangle and the coordinates are relabelled as {0,…,j}×{0,…,k}\{0,\ldots,j\}\times\{0,\ldots,k\}, the resulting cut weight is exactly that of the corresponding cut of 𝖧k​(dk)⊗𝖧j​(cj)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}). Hence Theorem 4.8 applies and gives

cut𝖧k​(dk)⊗𝖧j​(cj)≥h⁡(𝖧j​(cj))​h​(𝖧k​(dk)).\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})}\geq h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})).

By bilinearity of the Kronecker product,

𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)=∑j,kαj​βk​(𝒥b,k​(𝖧k​(dk))⊗𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(cj))).\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p)=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j}\beta_{k}\bigl(\mathcal{J}_{b,k}(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))\otimes\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}))\bigr).

For the fixed cut, the cut sum is linear in the matrix entries. Since the zero entries introduced by the embeddings do not contribute, the preceding blockwise bound yields

cut𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)\displaystyle\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p)} ≥∑j,kαj​βk​h​(𝖧j​(cj))​h​(𝖧k​(dk))\displaystyle\geq\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j}\beta_{k}h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}))h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))
=(∑jαj​h​(𝖧j​(cj)))​(∑kβk​h​(𝖧k​(dk))).\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}))\right)\left(\sum_{k}\beta_{k}h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))\right).

Since 𝒥a,j\mathcal{J}_{a,j} places the matrix in the lower-right corner and all entries outside the embedded block are zero, the last row sum of the embedded matrix is the same as that of the original matrix; thus h⁡(𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(cj)))=h⁡(𝖧j​(cj))h\bigl(\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}))\bigr)=h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})). By linearity of hh and the above decompositions, h⁡(𝖡a​(p))=∑jαj​h​(𝖧j​(cj))h(\mathsf{B}_{a}(p))=\sum_{j}\alpha_{j}h(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})) and h⁡(𝖡b​(q))=∑kβk​h​(𝖧k​(dk))h(\mathsf{B}_{b}(q))=\sum_{k}\beta_{k}h(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})). Consequently, cut𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)≥h⁡(𝖡a​(p))​h​(𝖡b​(q))\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p)}\geq h(\mathsf{B}_{a}(p))h(\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)). By (2.9), h⁡(𝖡a​(p))=ga​(p)h(\mathsf{B}_{a}(p))=g_{a}(p) and h⁡(𝖡b​(q))=gb​(q)h(\mathsf{B}_{b}(q))=g_{b}(q), and therefore

cut𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)−ga​(p)​gb​(q)≥0.\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p)}-g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q)\geq 0. (5.1)

It remains to determine when equality can occur. For the fixed global cut, bilinearity of 𝒬\mathcal{Q} and the above decompositions give

𝒬⁡(𝖡a​(p),𝖡b​(q))=∑j,kαj​βk​𝒬​(𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(cj)),𝒥b,k​(𝖧k​(dk))).\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{B}_{a}(p),\mathsf{B}_{b}(q))=\sum_{j,k}\alpha_{j}\beta_{k}\mathcal{Q}\!\left(\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})),\mathcal{J}_{b,k}(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))\right).

For each pair j,kj,k, restricting the fixed global cut to the corresponding lower-right rectangle and relabelling the coordinates yields a cut of 𝖧k​(dk)⊗𝖧j​(cj)\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k})\otimes\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}) that separates its two terminals. Since the embeddings introduce only zero rows and columns outside the blocks and preserve the last row sums,

𝒬⁡(𝒥a,j​(𝖧j​(cj)),𝒥b,k​(𝖧k​(dk)))=𝒬⁡(𝖧j​(cj),𝖧k​(dk))\mathcal{Q}\!\left(\mathcal{J}_{a,j}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j})),\mathcal{J}_{b,k}(\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))\right)=\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{j}(c_{j}),\mathsf{H}_{k}(d_{k}))

for this cut. Hence every term in the sum is nonnegative by Theorem 4.8.

Suppose now that the global cut is nonterminal. For j=aj=a and k=bk=b, the embeddings are trivial:

𝒥a,a​(𝖧a​(ca))=𝖧a​(ca),𝒥b,b​(𝖧b​(db))=𝖧b​(db).\mathcal{J}_{a,a}(\mathsf{H}_{a}(c_{a}))=\mathsf{H}_{a}(c_{a}),\qquad\mathcal{J}_{b,b}(\mathsf{H}_{b}(d_{b}))=\mathsf{H}_{b}(d_{b}).

Thus the corresponding term is

𝒬⁡(𝖧a​(ca),𝖧b​(db))\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{a}(c_{a}),\mathsf{H}_{b}(d_{b}))

for the original global cut itself. Since this cut is nonterminal, the equality assertion of Theorem 4.8 gives

𝒬⁡(𝖧a​(ca),𝖧b​(db))>0.\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{H}_{a}(c_{a}),\mathsf{H}_{b}(d_{b}))>0.

Since αa​βb>0\alpha_{a}\beta_{b}>0, while all the other terms in the sum are nonnegative, it follows that

𝒬⁡(𝖡a​(p),𝖡b​(q))>0.\mathcal{Q}(\mathsf{B}_{a}(p),\mathsf{B}_{b}(q))>0.

Equivalently,

cut𝖡b​(q)⊗𝖡a​(p)>ga​(p)​gb​(q)\operatorname{cut}_{\mathsf{B}_{b}(q)\otimes\mathsf{B}_{a}(p)}>g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q)

for every nonterminal cut.

Finally, by (2.9), the last row sums of 𝖡a​(p)\mathsf{B}_{a}(p) and 𝖡b​(q)\mathsf{B}_{b}(q) are ga​(p)g_{a}(p) and gb​(q)g_{b}(q), respectively. Hence the last row sum of their Kronecker product is ga​(p)​gb​(q)g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q). Since the matrices are symmetric, the last column sum has the same value. The two terminal cuts therefore attain equality in (5.1). ∎

Proof of Theorem A.

Because a+ba+b is even, the two exponents are either both odd or both even. Propositions 5.1 and 5.2 prove that every cut in Lemma 2.1 has weight at least γ=ga​(p)​gb​(q)\gamma=g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q), with equality exactly at the two terminal cuts. That lemma gives

maxyt=−1⁡F⁡(y)=pa​qb+da​(p)​db​(q)−2​ga​(p)​gb​(q),\max_{y_{t}=-1}F(y)=p^{a}q^{b}+d_{a}(p)d_{b}(q)-2g_{a}(p)g_{b}(q),

For y=−sy=-s, equation (2.5) gives xi,j=(1−(−1)i+j)/2x_{i,j}=(1-(-1)^{i+j})/2, so xx selects precisely 𝒟odd\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{odd}}. For y=s−2​ety=s-2e_{t}, it gives x=(𝟏+s)/2−etx=(\mathbf{1}+s)/2-e_{t}, which selects the even checkerboard and removes nn; this is 𝒟even−\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{even}}^{-}. Both sets contain proper divisors only: since a+ba+b is even, nn is absent from the first set and removed from the second. They are nonempty, because p,q∈𝒟oddp,q\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{odd}} and 1∈𝒟even−1\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{even}}^{-}.
